prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of topological insulators, the quantum spin Hall state and protected surface states in two and three dimensions

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are, for me, the cleanest example on the list of what the prize is for: an idea about band topology was predicted (the Z2 invariant and quantum spin Hall state), then found in nature, first as edge channels in HgTe quantum wells and then as protected surface states in bulk Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 crystals by ARPES. Nature gave the clues and the theory was confirmed rather than merely admired. The concept has reorganised how materials are classified and has spread to photonics, cold atoms, mechanics and superconductors. Two decades of independent confirmation make the interpretation stable, and recognition is timely and arguably overdue. It follows the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions without duplicating it, because that prize concerned topological order in model systems, whereas this is the discovery of a new class of real materials. A prize covering both the 2D and 3D realisations, with the Kane-Mele theory at its core, reads as one coherent discovery.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real. Mele is Kane's co-author on the decisive Z2 papers, and leaving him out is uncomfortable. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (who proposed the HgTe route) and Fu with Kane (3D) are outside the credited names. Hasan's 3D ARPES priority is not uncontested. With a three-person ceiling, any trio shortchanges someone, and a prize that looks arbitrary on attribution would damage an otherwise easy scientific case. The practical impact so far is also modest compared with the conceptual impact, and a sceptic could say this is a classification triumph more than a technology.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B032 first with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the most coherent theory-plus-experiment trio, and notes that Hasan's 3D ARPES work is a competing claim that his trio excludes.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on the discomfort over Mele, and I could live with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. My reason for keeping Hasan over Mele is that the prize should honour the discovery in nature in both dimensions. The 3D surface states are the step that made topological insulators a family of real materials rather than one fragile quantum-well result at millikelvin-scale devices. Mele's contribution is inseparable from Kane's on the theory, so a single theory name is defensible. Your trio drops the 3D confirmation, and I find that the larger loss. I would not make this a battle, but the committee should decide it explicitly rather than by default.

responses.point: Mehlig values B032 as a unifying mechanism in which band topology classifies phases, and rates B046 (twisted bilayer graphene) as probably premature because the superconducting mechanism and correlated states are unsettled.
responses.response: I share the view that B032 is the unifying idea, and I take the point on B046. I ranked B046 third because a theory-predicted flat band was found by experiment, which I value. But I accept that an unresolved pairing mechanism means a prize now would reward the observation, not an understood phenomenon, and I am sceptical of declaring a field settled when the central puzzle is still open. Where I disagree is the QKD point. You ranked B004 second and would credit the three theorists. That is a protocol prize, the 2022 entanglement prize already covers the foundational territory, and the physics discovery is thinner than in B032. I put it second in my opening for the quality of the ideas, but on reflection I would not defend it against the topological case.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B041) first as precision measurement that opens tests of relativity, varying constants and dark matter, and sees the Katori-Ye lineage as clean and mature.
responses.response: The attribution for B041 is indeed the cleanest on the table, and I like the link to gravity and to searches for new physics, so I ranked it only seventh because of how I weigh what has been learned. My reservation is that three of you put it first on the strength of what the clocks will enable, such as redefining the second and testing constants. So far, no deviation from known physics has been seen, and the 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured the comb and ion-control foundations. I would want to hear what the clocks have already taught us about nature, rather than how precisely they can measure. If the committee can articulate that, I would move it up. As it stands, it is my second alternative, not my first.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube's high-energy astrophysical neutrinos (B033) first as an instrument-driven opening of a new observational window with the diffuse flux, blazar association and Galactic-plane result.
responses.response: Of everything in the instrument category, this appeals to me most, because it is a clue from nature of the kind I want. I ranked it fifth, not first, because the sources of most events are still unidentified and the neutrino astronomy claim rests on two partial associations (TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068). The credit also troubles me: a two-name prize for a collaboration of hundreds, with the AMANDA founders and other IceCube leaders outside it. I would not oppose it in a few years once source identification is firmer, but I do not think it beats a field with twenty years of independent confirmation.

uncertainties: Whether Mele should displace Hasan (or Molenkamp) in the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp-Hasan configuration, and how the committee weighs Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu, who are outside the credited names.
Hasan's priority for the first 3D observation versus other ARPES groups, which I have not independently verified.
Whether the committee will prefer a single topological-insulator prize or would pair it with a second achievement; I have not found a second part that sits naturally with it.
Whether the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene will be clarified in time to change my view of B046.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My Princeton PhD supervisor, David Gross, and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are not credited in any shortlisted entry, and my own research (string theory and cosmology) is far from the condensed-matter, atomic and astroparticle candidates.
